More importantly, the slide characterises DVC as a 'lightweight Git-based tool', but the source says only 'independent open source tool focused on data scientists working with smaller datasets' — neither 'lightweight' nor 'Git-based' appear in the source excerpt.

pgvector vs. Dedicated Vector DB

claim_verdicts.bullet: **Dedicated engines** (e.g., Qdrant, Milvus) are the better choice when you need to scale beyond what a single Postgres instance handles or require advanced quantization features
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: pgvector is the better choice when you already run Postgres. Adding vector search is one migration, not a new service. Choose Qdrant when you need to scale beyond what a single Postgres instance handles or require advanced quantization features. A dedicated vector database provides real horizontal scaling across clusters and better performance for pure vector workloads, though this comes with the operational cost of maintaining a separate service.
claim_verdicts.issue: The source names only Qdrant as the dedicated engine example; the bullet adds Milvus as a second example without source support. The substantive claim (scaling/quantization as the decision axis) is fully supported, but Milvus is an unsourced addition.
claim_verdicts.suggested_fix: **Dedicated engines** (e.g., Qdrant) are the better choice when you need to scale beyond what a single Postgres instance handles or require advanced quantization features

Recap and Key Takeaways
Recap and Key Takeaways
claim_verdicts.bullet: Training-serving skew is caused by a discrepancy between how data is handled in training and serving pipelines, or by data changes between training and serving time
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: Training-serving skew is a difference between performance during training and performance during serving. This skew can be caused by: A discrepancy between how you handle data in the training and serving pipelines. A change in the data between when you train and when you serve. A feedback loop between your model and your algorithm.
claim_verdicts.issue: The source lists three causes of training-serving skew; the bullet omits the third — 'A feedback loop between your model and your algorithm.' While the bullet does not explicitly claim to be exhaustive, presenting only two of three named causes may mislead readers into thinking the list is complete.
claim_verdicts.suggested_fix: Training-serving skew is caused by a discrepancy between how data is handled in training and serving pipelines, by data changes between training and serving time, or by a feedback loop between the model and the serving algorithm

claim_verdicts.slide: Recap and Key Takeaways
claim_verdicts.bullet: A feature store prevents skew and feature duplication through shared transformation definitions applied identically across an offline store and an online store
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: One of the core functionalities of a feature store is its ability to store the logic as to how raw data was transformed into usable data, ensuring that all raw data coming from different sources are preprocessed using the same transformations, preventing training-serving skew. Transformation code is reused across environments preventing training-serving skew and frees teams from having to rewrite code from one environment to the next. Feature stores address training-serving skew by centralizing feature computation in a single pipeline that serves both offline and online stores.
claim_verdicts.issue: The bullet claims a feature store prevents 'feature duplication.' The source excerpts do not use this term or directly state this benefit. The source mentions preventing skew, reusing transformation code, and centralizing computation — but 'feature duplication' as a distinct problem prevented by a feature store is not stated. The claim may be inferrable but is not supported by the text.
claim_verdicts.suggested_fix: A feature store prevents training-serving skew through shared transformation definitions applied identically across an offline store and an online store, eliminating the need to rewrite feature computation logic for each environment

claim_verdicts.slide: Recap and Key Takeaways
Recap and Key Takeaways
claim_verdicts.bullet: Each embedding model defines its own coordinate system — changing the model invalidates all stored vectors and forces full re-embedding, creating de facto vendor lock-in
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: Each model defines its own coordinate system. Every vector already stored in your database becomes incompatible with your new model. When you embed 'quarterly revenue report' with OpenAI's ada-002, you get a specific 1536-dimensional point in space. When you embed the same text with text-embedding-3-large, you get a completely different 3072-dimensional point in a completely different space. If you update your query embeddings to the new model but forget to re-embed stored documents, your retrieval pipeline does not crash... Your system returns results — they are just wrong.
claim_verdicts.issue: The bullet adds 'creating de facto vendor lock-in' — a consequence not stated in the source. The source describes incompatibility and the need for re-embedding when switching models, but does not characterize this as 'vendor lock-in.' This is an editorial framing not supported by the excerpt.
claim_verdicts.suggested_fix: Each embedding model defines its own coordinate system — changing the model makes all stored vectors incompatible and forces full re-embedding of the entire corpus

claim_verdicts.slide: Recap and Key Takeaways
claim_verdicts.bullet: ANN recall is a silently violated SLO: as a vector database grows or parameters drift, retrieval quality degrades without raising errors while latency metrics remain stable
claim_verdicts.source_excerpt: As vector databases grow, retrieval quality deteriorates quietly—especially under approximate search—while latency metrics remain deceptively stable. This is a critical issue because a system that appears healthy from an infrastructure perspective gradually feeds weaker context to the LLM, increasing hallucinations and reducing answer quality. Going from 0.8 to 0.95 recall increased HNSW latency by roughly 31%, while IVF latency roughly tripled over the same recall range.
claim_verdicts.issue: The bullet adds 'or parameters drift' as a second cause of silent recall degradation alongside database growth. The source only mentions database growth ('as vector databases grow') as the cause; parameter drift is not stated. This introduces an unsupported additional causal mechanism.
claim_verdicts.suggested_fix: ANN recall is a silently violated SLO: as a vector database grows, retrieval quality degrades without raising errors while latency metrics remain stable
